claims.text: Low-temperature inhibition of precursor mobility governs the formation of noble-metal HEA nanoparticles through stochastic principles.
The inhibited-mobility process forces simultaneous reduction of multiple noble-metal precursors.
A five-noble-metal single-source precursor system can form single-phase HEA nanoparticles at low temperature.
The initial material is a well-mixed solution containing unreduced Pt, Pd, Ir, Ru, and Rh precursors.
Restricting atomic diffusion during nucleation promotes homogeneous alloy formation.
The resulting particles contain noble-metal atoms as isolated sites rather than contiguous clusters.
Increased linear CO adsorption and corresponding red shifts provide evidence of isolated noble-metal sites and charge transfer.
Stochastic incorporation places multiple noble metals within each nanoparticle.
Isolation of noble-metal sites modifies their local electronic or d-band structure.
The modified local electronic structure enhances chemisorption and catalytic turnover.
Binary alloys are more prone to cooperative reduction, phase segregation, and clustered active sites than five-element noble-metal HEAs.
Five-element noble-metal HEA nanoparticles synthesized under low-temperature, limited-mobility conditions will form a uniform single phase.
Five-element noble-metal HEA nanoparticles will have higher turnover frequency or lower overpotential than PtPd nanoparticles synthesized under identical conditions.
The proposed mechanism requires the noble-metal components to have sufficiently similar reduction kinetics.
Elevated temperature or prolonged residence time can invalidate the mechanism by increasing atomic mobility.
Large differences in component reduction potentials can invalidate stochastic homogeneous incorporation.
